Matric to University

By: Liz Fish | Production

Proposal


Show:

Unique Selling Point:
The 2018 national matric pass rate of 78% makes for fabulous headlines, but the reality is that the standard of matric has dropped, and the burden of the failure of the Basic and Higher Education system has simply been transferred to tertiary institutions. Matriculants now have access to free higher education, with all subjects now qualifying for a Bachelor’s pass, and expectations are running high. In an election year, tertiary education remains under enormous pressure to fulfil the dreams of the youth, and to address the massive unemployment rate. Already parties like the EFF are threatening disruption of the academic programme. The focus will be on students’ struggles and aspirations, and the reality of what tertiary educators have to accommodate.

Summary:
The matric pass rate of 2018 has been celebrated as a great success across the country, with a 78% pass rate, up from 2017’s 75% pass rate, but despite the heartfelt stories of students achieving matric passes against all odds, the reality behind the headlines remains dire. The real pass rate is closer to 50% if one accounts for all the students who started in grade one in 2007 and dropped out at Grade 10 or earlier. The number of bachelor passes has risen with more black matriculants achieving them, but for tertiary educators, the 2019 intake that arrives on their doorstep is as ill-equipped as in previous years. A bachelor’s pass which gives students access to university and technicons requires 40% in their home language, only 50% in four other subjects, and 30% in two other subjects. A matric doesn’t mean much any more.
The burden of the failure of the schooling system has been transferred onto tertiary institutions. Government has long recognised the need for bridging/development courses to help students cope with the demands of tertiary education - massive amounts of money are spent every year, but it’s still not enough. The through-put of students through tertiary institutions remains very low, either with high levels of dropouts or extended periods to obtain a basic degree – a three year degree plus one year often takes five or six years.


Further information:
Because the National Schools Certificate results are not a reflection of a student’s ability, universities have developed The National Benchmark Test (NBT) designed to assess their abilities beyond rote learning, and assess the more complex reasoning skills required in tertiary education. So a student who gets a high maths mark at school may still score a very poor mark in the NBT. Every year, 90 000 students write the NBTs in 120 venues across the country in both urban and rural settings. The data gleaned from this test is analysed and informs universities and technicons more accurately about that year’s cohort’s strengths and weaknesses. But NBT data does far more than screen/stream students: it informs bridging/development courses and curriculums – one example of this is that it was found that geometry was not taught at many schools.
Universities and Technicons have long recognised that if they are going to change the status quo, they need to get involved at a school level, either with teacher support or with direct student development. Others argue that high school intervention is already too late, and focus on the primary phase, teaching teachers to teach reading and numeracy. UCT’s 100Up programme operates in 20 schools across Khayelitsha identifying students with potential in maths and science and mentoring them from Grade 10. The programme runs tutorials, gives career advice, assists with applications and then supports the students through university.
Maths and science remain the critical skills and indicators of our education system. Mathematics develops logical reasoning and problem-solving, and is hence a “gateway” subject for many of the professions such as engineering, commerce and health sciences. But the state of maths and science remains dismal. The more selective universities require 80% and above for programmes in commerce, engineering, science, health sciences and quantitative social sciences. Of the roughly 5 500 students who wrote pure maths, only 2.6% got a distinction, and that’s what it takes to get into a degree at the top academic universities like Wits and UCT. But all universities have different requirements – the University of the Western Cape only requires students to get 55% and above, so they carry a massive burden of education development, as do the Technicons.
Now, as the excitement of the results fades, the reality of accessing your dream institution sets in. UCT had 62 740 applicants for 4 200 places; North West University, 52 000 applications for 9 391 places; Wits had 70 340 applications for 5 200 places; and Stellenbosch 34 000 applications for 5 300 places. But these figures need to be unpacked - some of these are the same applicants applying to three of four institutions, and often for courses for which they don’t have the basic requirements.
Aspirations of getting accepted for a degree at UCT, Wits, Stellenbosch or Pretoria in engineering, medicine, or commerce are high across all sectors. But the reality is that the 33% of matriculants who did achieve bachelors passes will have to settle for studying at one of the 22 other universities as each have different entrance requirements.

Script:


Phelisa “My name is Phelisa Maswana. My dream was to become a doctor
Amy- Lee Van der “I am Amy-Lee Van der Heyder I matriculated at Spine Road High and I want to be a lawyer
Aphelele “Hi I am Aphelele Nkantini and I was the top achiever at Chris Hani High School and I want to be a forensic scientist
Script: The class of 2018 did incredibly well with a 78% pass rate, and a 12% increase in Bachelors passes, what used to be known as a matric exemption. It’s the passport to apply to University.
UPsound Angie Mosheke “We can celebrate with pride that the majority of our learners passed well”
Script: But behind the political fanfare, senior researcher in educational policy Dr Nic Spaull says, we can’t forget the 600 000 students who started out in Grade one, who never made it to matric.
Nic: “We have 10 million South Africans that are unemployed. So even if you double the number of students that are going to university you've still got literally millions and millions of youth that don't have jobs they're never going to go to university
Script: Aphelele made it despite the odds, his parents in the Eastern Cape sent him to Cape Town to live with his brother to get a better education
Mac “ So it must have been tough for you studying without your parents around
Apelele “Yeah It was bad. It really was. Yeah. Growing up without my parents joh it’s not a good thing for a black child you know, you have to have that support from the parents
Mac “So what's your dream. What do you want to be?
Aplelele “One day I want to go to become a forensic scientist. I want to use my scientific intelligence to catch the bad guys
Script: Amy-Lee grew up in Tafelsig Mitchels Plein with her grandparents in an extremely rough neighbourhood. She dreams of justice
Amy- lee: “I want to do law. I've been involved in unfair matters, and I was treated unfairly and I was like now I want to be a lawyer because of this
Script: Fresh out the school gate, with their heads filled with big dreams, the reality of what their 12 years of education has actually equipped them with, is sinking in.
Philisa “I wanted to study and be a medicine in general but at UCT they reject me , so you UWC I applied to for chemical sciences to do chemistry so they accept me
Awetu: I passed with a bachelor pass with 3 distinctions. At UWC I applied for pharmacy and in CPUT and UWC I applied for emergency medical care.
Mac Have you had any responses?
Awetu: “I didn't meet the requirements at UCT. CPUT and UWC I did, but they rejected me I don’t know why
LINK “This is the story of many young South Africans, they leave matric with not only their hopes and aspirations, but that of their families, but the harsh reality of entering tertiary institutions is really daunting
Nic:” Universities enrolment has only been increasing by I think three to five percent each year but the number of bachelor passes that are being additional bachelor passes that are being produced each year is much much higher than that. So that's why you have more and more students that are frustrated that they're not getting places at university despite the fact that they've got a bachelor's pass.
LINK “In 2018 the Department of education dropped the list of specialised subjects, and now you can get a bachelors pass with a 50% in dance, tourism or maths lit, this has raised the number of bachelors passes and the expectations to get into University
Nic “In April of 2018 they changed the rules about what constitutes a bachelor's pass. [12:06:14] This is the first year that subjects like that qualified you to go to university. Now whether the universities accept those students or not is another question.
Script: Expectations are running high, and the EFF is adding to the pressure
EFF “If the University doesn’t allow walk in then that means no one must enter that campus
Script: UWC Deputy Registrar Ahmed Shaikjee is bracing himself as registration across the country begins this week
Ahmed Shaikjee “In terms of the EFF statement we do allow walk in applicants. We do even accept quite a few of them but we will never be able to accommodate all learners with a bachelor's pass. So if you're looking at the Faculty of Dentistry you cannot just say that ever walked in we will accept them because there is only a certain number of lab space they’re not going to get the quality of education and training that we need to give them
LINK “Across the country every year 100’s of 1000s of learners students have applied to tertiary institutions, however there just isn’t enough space. Almost every institution gets 14 times the number of applications than they can actually accommodate
Script: The numbers are staggering: at UCT there are 62 740 applications for 4 200 places. WITS
70 340 applications for 5 200 places, UKZN 100 000 for 8770
Script: Registrar Mr Nikile Ntsababa of Cape Peninsular University of Technology, says they cater for the most students of all institutions in the Western Cape
Registrar: We've received close to 38 000 thousand students of those 9437 meet our requirements. The rest of the student do not meet our requirements
Script: Most students apply to several institutions which accounts for some of the extremely high figures. Naziema Jappie of the Centre for Educational testing and access placement- CETAP, says the Department of Education has an online system which hopes to streamline the process
Naziema: So there is the central application systems basically means that students will apply to one application centre. And that means that a student applies to maybe 10 different kinds of institutions. Some institutions charge and application fees and some don't. So the central application fee is just one fee that the student will pay. And we'll be able to apply through that system.
Script: But it’s not a silver bullet if you want to go to University and you meet the requirements. These students are still in the dark about their options
Awetu: All of them now they say they like me met their requirements. But they have been rejected so I feel like there is something wrong.
Mac: But why varsity though why...
Roxanne: Because our previous teachers also wanted us to go to Varsity always talking about Vartsity varsity so we're want to go there.
Mac: “So you didn't look at any other options you know technical colleges and those kind of things.
Roxanne: “We did Not as much as we want to go to go to varsity
Script: Often students have none, or the incorrect career advice, and even with a bachelors pass, they don’t meet the standards, and would fare better in Technical or Vocational colleges
Nic: I like to think of TVET colleges as being the kind of ugly stepchild of high education. They have serious infrastructure backlogs. The growth rates and TVET colleges have been multiples of the growth rates in universities.
Script: The National Senior Certificate isn’t necessarily an indication of a student’s ability to handle the rigors of tertiary education, so Universities of South Africa developed the National Bench Mark test. It’s run by CETAP, an independent body that tested 85 000 first-year applicants across the country in 2018.
Naizeema “The national benchmark test is one of those tests that looks at the achievements of students in terms of mathematics, academic literacy and quantitative literacy. And one is able to say what kind of students we are getting into Institutions. Are these students ready for university? And what the NBT tells us is what kind of support we then need to give these particular students.
Script: The limitations of their basic education really hits home when students enter tertiary institutions
Nic “I think Maths is also a really good indicator of the problems that we have in the system. 78% of maths Grade 6 math teachers in the country can't do grade 6 maths themselves. So if we look at the 2018 matric results about they've got at least 30% in maths or maths literacy. That means that only about 36 % of students of that starting cohort are passing maths at matric.
Script: And it’s institutions like CPUT and UWC, which are carrying the biggest load. Dr Mark Jacobs heads up a Maths development project at CPUT. The minimum requirements for Engineering are 50% in Maths Science and English
Mark: Of course a 50% pass in mathematics and science is an indication that 50% of the work was not done well. I'll give a good example trigonometry which is fundamental in some of my engineering programs, we find that the students haven't done it either haven't done it or haven't done sufficiently at school.
Script: UWC’s Dean of Science, Professor Michael Davies-Coleman says they are struggling to fill spaces in courses that require 50% in maths and science
Davies-Coleman: [09:12:37] It is important that we fill our targets because the country needs scientists mathematicians and specifically statisticians at this stage. We're talking about the fourth industrial revolution with large data sets massive data sets
Script: CPUT gets funding for extended programs for 15% of their students, but 80% need some form of support.
Mark “It is a very very hard transition especially in the first semester. And we do have a high failure rate.
Script: UWC have changed their teaching methods, and extended their support program into 2nd year which is seeing results, the pass rates have increased to 67%. But the throughput rate across all institutions, remains low.
Dean So we have to continually give confidence and say yes you can yes you can do this. It requires the students to take ownership of their own education.
Script: But the leap from school and their communities is enormous. The majority of students have never seen the universities they heading for
Mac” Apelel what are your greatest fears.
Apelele “having to adjust to my new life now, having to study at University, make new friends meet new people, I think that will be very difficult ja
Mac “All the best man and good luck, I hope you really do well- all the best
Script: The Class of 2018 could be in for a tough year with elections around the corner and despite NSFAS funding having increased to R24 billion this year, there are many disappointed class mates who qualified to study but just can’t find a place

At UWC I applied for pharmacy and in CPUT and UWC I applied for emergency medical care. Mac Have you had any responses? Awetu: “I didn't meet the requirements at UCT. CPUT and UWC I did, but they rejected me I don’t know why LINK “This is the story of many young South Africans, they leave matric with not only their hopes and aspirations, but that of their families, but the harsh reality of entering tertiary institutions is really daunting Nic:” Universities enrolment has only been increasing by I think three to five percent each year but the number of bachelor passes that are being additional bachelor passes that are being produced each year is much much higher than that. So that's why you have more and more students that are frustrated that they're not getting places at university despite the fact that they've got a bachelor's pass. LINK “In 2018 the Department of education dropped the list of specialised subjects, and now you can get a bachelors pass with a 50% in dance, tourism or maths lit, this has raised the number of bachelors passes and the expectations to get into University Nic “In April of 2018 they changed the rules about what constitutes a bachelor's pass. [12:06:14] This is the first year that subjects like that qualified you to go to university. Now whether the universities accept those students or not is another question. Script: Expectations are running high, and the EFF is adding to the pressure EFF “If the University doesn’t allow walk in then that means no one must enter that campus Script: UWC Deputy Registrar Ahmed Shaikjee is bracing himself as registration across the country begins this week Ahmed Shaikjee “In terms of the EFF statement we do allow walk in applicants. We do even accept quite a few of them but we will never be able to accommodate all learners with a bachelor's pass. So if you're looking at the Faculty of Dentistry you cannot just say that ever walked in we will accept them because there is only a certain number of lab space they’re not going to get the quality of education and training that we need to give them LINK “Across the country every year 100’s of 1000s of learners students have applied to tertiary institutions, however there just isn’t enough space. Almost every institution gets 14 times the number of applications than they can actually accommodate Script: The numbers are staggering: at UCT there are 62 740 applications for 4 200 places. WITS 70 340 applications for 5 200 places, UKZN 100 000 for 8770 Script: Registrar Mr Nikile Ntsababa of Cape Peninsular University of Technology, says they cater for the most students of all institutions in the Western Cape Registrar: We've received close to 38 000 thousand students of those 9437 meet our requirements. The rest of the student do not meet our requirements Script: Most students apply to several institutions which accounts for some of the extremely high figures. Naziema Jappie of the Centre for Educational testing and access placement- CETAP, says the Department of Education has an online system which hopes to streamline the process Naziema: So there is the central application systems basically means that students will apply to one application centre. And that means that a student applies to maybe 10 different kinds of institutions. Some institutions charge and application fees and some don't. So the central application fee is just one fee that the student will pay. And we'll be able to apply through that system. Script: But it’s not a silver bullet if you want to go to University and you meet the requirements. These students are still in the dark about their options Awetu: All of them now they say they like me met their requirements. But they have been rejected so I feel like there is something wrong. Mac: But why varsity though why... Roxanne: Because our previous teachers also wanted us to go to Varsity always talking about Vartsity varsity so we're want to go there. Mac: “So you didn't look at any other options you know technical colleges and those kind of things. Roxanne: “We did Not as much as we want to go to go to varsity Script: Often students have none, or the incorrect career advice, and even with a bachelors pass, they don’t meet the standards, and would fare better in Technical or Vocational colleges Nic: I like to think of TVET colleges as being the kind of ugly stepchild of high education. They have serious infrastructure backlogs. The growth rates and TVET colleges have been multiples of the growth rates in universities. Script: The National Senior Certificate isn’t necessarily an indication of a student’s ability to handle the rigors of tertiary education, so Universities of South Africa developed the National Bench Mark test. It’s run by CETAP, an independent body that tested 85 000 first-year applicants across the country in 2018. Naizeema “The national benchmark test is one of those tests that looks at the achievements of students in terms of mathematics, academic literacy and quantitative literacy. And one is able to say what kind of students we are getting into Institutions. Are these students ready for university? And what the NBT tells us is what kind of support we then need to give these particular students. Script: The limitations of their basic education really hits home when students enter tertiary institutions Nic “I think Maths is also a really good indicator of the problems that we have in the system. 78% of maths Grade 6 math teachers in the country can't do grade 6 maths themselves. So if we look at the 2018 matric results about they've got at least 30% in maths or maths literacy. That means that only about 36 % of students of that starting cohort are passing maths at matric. Script: And it’s institutions like CPUT and UWC, which are carrying the biggest load. Dr Mark Jacobs heads up a Maths development project at CPUT. The minimum requirements for Engineering are 50% in Maths Science and English Mark: Of course a 50% pass in mathematics and science is an indication that 50% of the work was not done well. I'll give a good example trigonometry which is fundamental in some of my engineering programs, we find that the students haven't done it either haven't done it or haven't done sufficiently at school. Script: UWC’s Dean of Science, Professor Michael Davies-Coleman says they are struggling to fill spaces in courses that require 50% in maths and science Davies-Coleman: [09:12:37] It is important that we fill our targets because the country needs scientists mathematicians and specifically statisticians at this stage. We're talking about the fourth industrial revolution with large data sets massive data sets Script: CPUT gets funding for extended programs for 15% of their students, but 80% need some form of support. Mark “It is a very very hard transition especially in the first semester. And we do have a high failure rate. Script: UWC have changed their teaching methods, and extended their support program into 2nd year which is seeing results, the pass rates have increased to 67%. But the throughput rate across all institutions, remains low. Dean So we have to continually give confidence and say yes you can yes you can do this. It requires the students to take ownership of their own education. Script: But the leap from school and their communities is enormous. The majority of students have never seen the universities they heading for Mac” Apelel what are your greatest fears. Apelele “having to adjust to my new life now, having to study at University, make new friends meet new people, I think that will be very difficult ja Mac “All the best man and good luck, I hope you really do well- all the best Script: The Class of 2018 could be in for a tough year with elections around the corner and despite NSFAS funding having increased to R24 billion this year, there are many disappointed class mates who qualified to study but just can’t find a place

metadata.Unique Selling Point: The 2018 national matric pass rate of 78% makes for fabulous headlines, but the reality is that the standard of matric has dropped, and the burden of the failure of the Basic and Higher Education system has simply been transferred to tertiary institutions. Matriculants now have access to free higher education, with all subjects now qualifying for a Bachelor’s pass, and expectations are running high. In an election year, tertiary education remains under enormous pressure to fulfil the dreams of the youth, and to address the massive unemployment rate. Already parties like the EFF are threatening disruption of the academic programme. The focus will be on students’ struggles and aspirations, and the reality of what tertiary educators have to accommodate.
metadata.Summary: The matric pass rate of 2018 has been celebrated as a great success across the country, with a 78% pass rate, up from 2017’s 75% pass rate, but despite the heartfelt stories of students achieving matric passes against all odds, the reality behind the headlines remains dire. The real pass rate is closer to 50% if one accounts for all the students who started in grade one in 2007 and dropped out at Grade 10 or earlier. The number of bachelor passes has risen with more black matriculants achieving them, but for tertiary educators, the 2019 intake that arrives on their doorstep is as ill-equipped as in previous years. A bachelor’s pass which gives students access to university and technicons requires 40% in their home language, only 50% in four other subjects, and 30% in two other subjects. A matric doesn’t mean much any more. The burden of the failure of the schooling system has been transferred onto tertiary institutions. Government has long recognised the need for bridging/development courses to help students cope with the demands of tertiary education - massive amounts of money are spent every year, but it’s still not enough. The through-put of students through tertiary institutions remains very low, either with high levels of dropouts or extended periods to obtain a basic degree – a three year degree plus one year often takes five or six years.
metadata.Further information: Because the National Schools Certificate results are not a reflection of a student’s ability, universities have developed The National Benchmark Test (NBT) designed to assess their abilities beyond rote learning, and assess the more complex reasoning skills required in tertiary education. So a student who gets a high maths mark at school may still score a very poor mark in the NBT. Every year, 90 000 students write the NBTs in 120 venues across the country in both urban and rural settings. The data gleaned from this test is analysed and informs universities and technicons more accurately about that year’s cohort’s strengths and weaknesses. But NBT data does far more than screen/stream students: it informs bridging/development courses and curriculums – one example of this is that it was found that geometry was not taught at many schools. Universities and Technicons have long recognised that if they are going to change the status quo, they need to get involved at a school level, either with teacher support or with direct student development. Others argue that high school intervention is already too late, and focus on the primary phase, teaching teachers to teach reading and numeracy. UCT’s 100Up programme operates in 20 schools across Khayelitsha identifying students with potential in maths and science and mentoring them from Grade 10. The programme runs tutorials, gives career advice, assists with applications and then supports the students through university. Maths and science remain the critical skills and indicators of our education system. Mathematics develops logical reasoning and problem-solving, and is hence a “gateway” subject for many of the professions such as engineering, commerce and health sciences. But the state of maths and science remains dismal. The more selective universities require 80% and above for programmes in commerce, engineering, science, health sciences and quantitative social sciences. Of the roughly 5 500 students who wrote pure maths, only 2.6% got a distinction, and that’s what it takes to get into a degree at the top academic universities like Wits and UCT. But all universities have different requirements – the University of the Western Cape only requires students to get 55% and above, so they carry a massive burden of education development, as do the Technicons. Now, as the excitement of the results fades, the reality of accessing your dream institution sets in. UCT had 62 740 applicants for 4 200 places; North West University, 52 000 applications for 9 391 places; Wits had 70 340 applications for 5 200 places; and Stellenbosch 34 000 applications for 5 300 places. But these figures need to be unpacked - some of these are the same applicants applying to three of four institutions, and often for courses for which they don’t have the basic requirements. Aspirations of getting accepted for a degree at UCT, Wits, Stellenbosch or Pretoria in engineering, medicine, or commerce are high across all sectors. But the reality is that the 33% of matriculants who did achieve bachelors passes will have to settle for studying at one of the 22 other universities as each have different entrance requirements.
